# Fitting models

To find out which model gives the best trade-off between bias and variance, between
accuracy and flexibility, one strategy is to fit both a flexible and a more rigid model
and determine from the CV error which direction on the flexibility axis we should go to
avoid overtraining.

We'll consider classification trees and random forests. Random forests are probably the
least prone to overtraining, and are considered one of the best "off-the-shelf" machine
learning algorithms, in the sense that they require little expertise to apply and
perform well without tuning. (That's not to say that tuning shouldn't be considered!)
It's your Uncle Bob's favorite algorithm, so to speak.

```{r model-functions, code=unlist(lapply(list.files("R/models", pattern="\\.R$", full.names=TRUE), readLines)), fold="Model fitting functions", message=FALSE}
for (file in list.files("R/models", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) {
  source(file, local = TRUE)
}
```

```{r classification-functions, code=readLines("R/evaluation/classification.R"), fold="Classification evaluation function", message=FALSE}
source("R/evaluation/classification.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r resampling-settings}
set.seed(2023)
subjects <- sub("_.*", "", basename(rownames(x_train)))
folds <- caret::groupKFold(subjects, k = 5)
control <- caret::trainControl("cv", 5, index = folds, allowParallel = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-models}
training <- train_models(features_train, y, control, seed = 2023)
models <- training$models
models

## Report execution time
training$timings
```

```{r compare-models}
## Compare models on the same folds
resampling <- caret::resamples(models)
model_comparison <- summary(resampling)$statistics$Accuracy |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("model") |>
  dplyr::select(model, accuracy = Mean) |>
  dplyr::left_join(training$timings, by = "model") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(accuracy))
model_comparison
```

As always, it's useful to check how well the algorithm performs on the training set: If
it doesn't classify the training set accurately, how can you expect better results on
the test set? This seemingly obvious point is often overlooked—surprisingly.

```{r evaluate-models}
## Check performance on training set
training_performance <- lapply(models, function(model) {
  predictions <- predict(model, features_train, type = "raw")
  evaluate_classification(predictions, y)
})
training_performance
```
